title: Adolescent Mental Health in Families Affected by Parental Substance Use
content: Background and Objective: Living with parents diagnosed with substance use disorder (SUD) constitutes a critical stressor for healthy child and adolescent development. This study empirically analyzes the impact of parental SUD on mental health, academic performance, and addictive behaviors in adolescence. Method: A cross-sectional quasi-experimental design was implemented with a sample of 40 adolescents (20 in the experimental group exposed to parental SUD and 20 in the control group). Emotional and behavioral dimensions were assessed using a validated psychometric battery (BDI-II, STAI, RSE, CBCL, CRAFFT, CERM/CERI) and a review of academic records. Hypotheses were tested using nonparametric statistics (Mann-Whitney U test and Fisher’s exact test). Results: The experimental group showed clinically, and statistically higher levels of depression, state-trait anxiety, and behavioral problems compared to the control group. A drastic decline in academic performance and significantly lower self-esteem was observed. The pattern of imitation and vulnerability found is alarming: 75% of the adolescents exposed to s are at high risk for early drug use, and they also exhibit abusive use of cell phones as a mechanism for emotional refuge. Conclusions: Parental SUD goes beyond mere systemic dysfunction, acting as a factor that hinders psychosocial maturation and reinforces patterns of passive coping, maladjustment, and emotional dysregulation in the child. These findings warn of the imminent risk of intergenerational transmission of addiction, underscoring the urgency of implementing targeted prevention programs focused on breaking this traumatic cycle.
